# QuickOper

> Verified-calculation tools. Every calculation runs entirely in the visitor's
> browser; no input is transmitted, logged or stored.
>
> Two verticals: /finance (personal money decisions) and /machining (metric-first
> shop-floor calculations). They share a verification method and nothing else.

QuickOper computes, it does not advise. Each tool performs deterministic
arithmetic and publishes its formula, its intermediate values, a full
period-by-period schedule, and the fixture tests proving its output matches a
real published third-party figure.

Nothing on this site is financial, tax or investment advice. The expertise
claimed is computational, not advisory.

## Tools — finance

### Debt payoff calculator — avalanche vs snowball
URL: https://quickoper.com/finance/debt-payoff-calculator
Computes: months to debt freedom and total interest, for the avalanche and
snowball strategies and for a minimum-payments-only baseline, with a full
month-by-month schedule.
Inputs: per-debt balance, annual rate and minimum payment; one total monthly
payment.
Jurisdiction: none. Interest is charged monthly on the opening balance, which
is a convention, not a rule of any one country.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify

### Coast FIRE calculator
URL: https://quickoper.com/finance/coast-fire-calculator
Computes: the amount that must already be invested for it to reach a retirement
target with no further contributions, plus a year-by-year projection.
Inputs: current age, retirement age, amount invested, annual spending,
withdrawal rate, real annual return, monthly contribution.
Jurisdiction: none. No tax treatment or account type is modelled.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify

### Mortgage overpayment calculator
URL: https://quickoper.com/finance/mortgage-overpayment-calculator
Computes: what an extra monthly payment removes from a fixed-rate mortgage, in
months and in interest, with the full month-by-month amortisation schedule.
Inputs: amount borrowed, annual interest rate, term in years, extra paid monthly.
Jurisdiction: US fixed-rate convention. Interest is charged monthly at
annualRate/12, which is how a lender's nominal APR is defined.
Key figures, computed on $320,000 at 6.706% over 30 years:
  - Required monthly payment: $2,066.16. This matches calculator.net's
    published output for the same inputs, to the cent.
  - Contractual schedule: 360 payments, $423,821.51 of interest.
  - Paying $200 extra a month: 280 payments, $312,930.95 of interest.
  - That removes 80 months and $110,890.56 of interest.
  - Month 1 on the contractual payment: $1,788.27 interest, $277.89 principal.
  - The final payment is $2,070.07, larger than the others, because a payment
    rounded to the cent leaves a residue that lenders collect in the last month
    rather than issuing a 361st bill.
Not modelled: escrow, PMI, fees, prepayment penalties, adjustable rates.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify

### UK early repayment charge calculator
URL: https://quickoper.com/finance/uk-early-repayment-charge-calculator
Computes: what a UK early repayment charge costs against the interest an
overpayment removes, reported on two separate horizons — the months the rate is
contractually fixed, and the whole remaining term.
Inputs: outstanding balance, interest rate, years left, months left on the fixed
rate, annual penalty-free overpayment allowance (%), early repayment charge (%),
and the overpayment being considered.
Jurisdiction: United Kingdom. A UK fixed deal allows a percentage of the balance
to be repaid each year without penalty and charges a percentage of the excess —
a different contractual rule from a US fixed-rate note, which is why it is a
separate tool rather than a currency switch.
No lender's terms are assumed. The allowance and the charge are both INPUTS,
because they vary by lender, product and year of the deal. FCA MCOB 12.3.1R
requires an early repayment charge to be "able to be expressed as a cash value"
and "a reasonable pre-estimate of the costs", so the figure is stated on the
borrower's own offer.
Key figures, on an illustrative £250,000 at 4.5% with 25 years left, 36 months
still fixed, a 10% allowance and a 3% charge, overpaying £40,000:
  - Penalty-free allowance £25,000, so £15,000 is chargeable and the charge is
    £450.00.
  - Interest removed WITHIN the 36 contractually fixed months: £5,598.91. Net of
    the charge, £5,148.91 ahead. This figure rests on no assumption.
  - Interest removed over the whole 25 years IF the rate never changed:
    £66,028.22, and 76 months off the schedule. That horizon assumes a rate that
    expires in 36 months and is labelled as such.
  - The comparison reverses on the two things borrowers rarely check. At 1.5%
    with 6 months of the deal left and a 5% charge, overpaying £50,000 costs
    £1,250.00 and removes only £313.29 inside the fixed period — £936.71 behind,
    with the crossing point at £28,581.69.
  - Rule of thumb the arithmetic produces: a charge is a one-off percentage,
    while the saving is the rate working over the months still fixed. So compare
    the charge percentage against the rate multiplied by the years left on the
    deal.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify

## Derivations

### How long minimum payments take, and when they never finish
URL: https://quickoper.com/minimum-payments
States: a minimum payment reduces a credit card balance only if it is larger
than that month's interest. Interest is balance x (APR / 12); the balance moves
by (interest - payment). If the payment is smaller than the interest the balance
rises every month and the card never clears, regardless of how long payments
continue. There is no third case.
Key figures, all computed at build time by the same engine the debt payoff
calculator runs, assuming a fixed monthly payment and no further spending:
  - $3,000 at 29.99% APR charges $74.98 of interest in month one. A $30
    payment leaves the balance $44.98 HIGHER than before it. The card never
    reaches zero.
  - The stand-still payment - the amount that holds a balance exactly level and
    repays nothing - is balance x (APR / 12). On $3,000 at 29.99% that is
    $74.98 a month.
  - $3,000 at 29.99% paying $90 a month clears in 73 months and costs
    $3,526.99 of interest, which is $526.99 MORE than the balance itself.
  - $6,000 at 22.99% paying $150 a month clears in 77 months, costing
    $5,492.03 of interest.
  - The same $6,000 at $250 a month clears in 33 months, costing $2,113.21.
    An extra $100 a month removes 44 months and $3,378.82 of interest.
  - These are the OPTIMISTIC figures. Issuers commonly set the minimum as a
    percentage of the balance, which shrinks as the balance falls, so a real
    minimum payment takes longer than a fixed payment of the same starting
    amount.

### How credit card interest is actually calculated
URL: https://quickoper.com/credit-card-interest
States: a credit card daily periodic rate is APR divided by 365. At 22.99% APR
that is 0.062986% per day. Interest is charged on the average daily balance of
the billing cycle, not the closing balance.
Key figures, all computed on a $6,000 balance at 22.99% APR:
  - 28-day cycle: $105.82. 30-day cycle: $113.38. 31-day cycle: $117.15.
  - APR/12 monthly approximation: $114.95 per month.
  - Over a full year both methods total exactly $1,379.40.
  - With daily compounding, one year costs $1,550.30 - an effective annual
    rate of 25.838% against a stated 22.99%.
  - A $200 payment on a 30-day cycle costs $109.60 of interest if it lands on
    day 1 and $113.25 if it lands on day 30.

### Why a 7% return is not 0.583% a month
URL: https://quickoper.com/monthly-return-rate
States: converting a stated annual RETURN to a monthly rate requires the twelfth
root, not division by twelve. A 7% annual return is 0.565415% per month, being
(1.07)^(1/12) - 1. Dividing gives 0.583333%, which compounds to an effective
7.2290% per year rather than 7%.
Key figures:
  - $100,000 for 30 years at a stated 7%: $761,225.50 using the twelfth root,
    $811,649.75 using r/12. The error overstates by $50,424.24, or 6.62%.
  - The error is always in the flattering direction.
  - An APR is the exception: a lender APR is a nominal rate defined as twelve
    times the monthly rate, so dividing by twelve is correct for debt.
  - Real return is nominal divided by inflation, not minus: 8% nominal against
    3% inflation is (1.08/1.03)-1 = 4.854369%, not 5%. Over 30 years on
    $100,000 that is $414,568.14 against $432,194.24.

### Where the 4% rule comes from, and what it does not say
URL: https://quickoper.com/withdrawal-rate
States: a withdrawal rate converts annual spending into a savings target by
dividing 100 by the rate. 4% is 25 times spending; 3% is 33.33 times.
Key figures, computed on $40,000 of annual spending:
  - 4% -> $1,000,000. 3.5% -> $1,142,857.14. 3% -> $1,333,333.33.
  - Moving from 4% to 3% adds 8.33x spending, a 33.3% increase in capital,
    because the multiple is 1/rate and therefore a hyperbola.
  - Bengen (1994) tested 30-year windows in US market history. The finding was
    never tested for longer retirements, other markets, or after fees and tax.
  - Sequence-of-returns risk, demonstrated: the same ten annual returns applied
    in opposite orders to a $1,000,000 portfolio drawing $40,000 a year end
    $1,573,834.11 (bad years first) against $1,835,954.59 (good years first) -
    $262,120.48 apart on an identical 10% arithmetic mean.

### What a coast number is, and what it is not
URL: https://quickoper.com/coast-number
States: a coast number is target / (1 + real return)^years - the amount that must
already be invested for compounding alone to reach a retirement target with no
further contributions. Passing it makes further SAVING optional, not working.
Key figures, on a $1,000,000 target:
  - At 5% real: 40 years out $142,045.68; 30 years $231,377.45; 20 years
    $376,889.48; 10 years $613,913.25; 5 years $783,526.17.
  - Sensitivity to the assumed return, 30 years out: 7% gives $131,367.12,
    5% gives $231,377.45, 3% gives $411,986.76. The pessimistic assumption
    needs more than three times the capital of the optimistic one.
  - The return must be a REAL return if the target is in today's money.
  - It cannot express sequence-of-returns risk; it is a single discount at a
    constant rate.

### Biweekly mortgage payments — what the thirteenth payment actually does
URL: https://quickoper.com/biweekly-mortgage-payments
States: twenty-six half-payments a year is thirteen monthly payments, not
twelve. The whole benefit of a biweekly schedule is that one extra payment; the
fortnightly timing contributes almost nothing.
Key figures, computed on $320,000 at 6.706% over 30 years:
  - Contractual monthly payment $2,066.16. Twelve of those is $24,793.92 a year;
    twenty-six halves is $26,860.08 - a difference of $2,066.16, exactly one
    payment.
  - That one extra payment a year removes 72 months and $99,532.52 of interest.
  - On the CFPB's own example loan from its Nationwide Biweekly enforcement
    action, $160,000 at 4.125%, the extra payment removes $18,840.18 of interest.
  - Not modelled: a true fortnightly accrual, where half a payment lands
    mid-month. That effect is real and small beside the thirteenth payment.

### What an extra payment does in year one versus year twenty
URL: https://quickoper.com/mortgage-overpayment-timing
States: the value of an extra mortgage payment depends on how much of the term
is left in front of it, because interest is charged on the balance every
remaining month. A dollar retired in month 1 escapes 359 future interest
charges; the same dollar retired in month 241 escapes 119.
Key figures, computed on $320,000 at 6.706% over 30 years, payment $2,066.16:
  - $5,000 paid once in month 1 removes $30,332.98 of interest and 17 months.
    The same $5,000 in month 121 removes $13,523.40 and 8 months. In month 241
    it removes $4,604.94 and 4 months. Identical amount, 6.6 times the effect.
  - The first payment is 86.6% interest: $1,788.27 interest against $277.89 of
    principal. By month 240 it is 49.0%: $1,013.44 against $1,052.72.
  - Principal first exceeds interest in month 237, more than two-thirds of the
    way through a 30-year term.
  - The balance falls $3,439.16 in year one, $12,253.56 in year twenty and
    $23,919.98 in year thirty - for twelve identical payments each time.
  - Not modelled: recasting, early repayment charges, or a servicer holding
    extra money in suspense rather than applying it to principal.

### What a 15-year mortgage costs against a 30-year
URL: https://quickoper.com/15-year-vs-30-year-mortgage
States: at the same interest rate, halving the term raises the payment by about
a third and removes more than half the interest. Both loans are charged
identical interest in month one, because interest is charged on the balance and
on day one the balance and rate are the same.
Key figures, computed on $320,000 at 6.706%, the same rate applied to both terms:
  - 30 years: payment $2,066.16, interest $423,821.51, total $743,821.51.
  - 15 years: payment $2,823.91, interest $188,303.66, total $508,303.66.
  - The payment is 36.7% higher; the interest is 55.6% lower, a difference of
    $235,517.85.
  - Month one on BOTH loans charges $1,788.27 of interest. The 30-year retires
    $277.89 of principal, the 15-year $1,035.64 - 3.7 times as much from a
    payment only 36.7% larger.
  - Principal first exceeds interest in month 237 on the 30-year and month 57 on
    the 15-year.
  - The borrower hands over 2.32 times the amount borrowed over 30 years and
    1.59 times over 15.
  - Paying the 15-year amount on a 30-year contract clears it in 180 months
    having charged $188,303.66 - identical to a real 15-year loan, to the cent.
    At a fixed rate the term is the payment.
  - The rate is deliberately held constant across both terms. Lenders normally
    price 15-year products lower, which would widen every gap above; no 15-year
    quote is invented here.

## Tools — machining

Metric-first calculations for machining. The drill catalogues are GENERATED from
their series definitions rather than transcribed from a table, so no individual
diameter is a value someone copied. Series that WOULD require transcription —
number drills, letter drills, the DIN 338 R40 preferred series, and named thread
presets — are deliberately absent until a person has verified them against a
manufacturer catalogue, and each page names what is missing.

### Machining calculators (hub)
URL: https://quickoper.com/machining
Computes: nothing directly; indexes the machining tools.
Inputs: none.
Jurisdiction: none. ISO metric and Unified inch thread forms are international.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify

### The machinist Android app (in development)
URL: https://quickoper.com/machining/app
Computes: nothing. It describes an unreleased Android app and asks machinists
whether it is worth building.
Inputs: none.
Status: IN DEVELOPMENT, NOT RELEASED. There is no price to pay, no pre-order and
no download. The page carries no purchasable offer for that reason.
Key figures: intended price $19.99 one-time, no subscription, no ads, no
account. That figure comes from Play Store reviews of competing apps in which
machinists stated what they would pay and refused a subscription.
Jurisdiction: none.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify

### Tap drill calculator
URL: https://quickoper.com/machining/tap-drill-calculator
Computes: the largest drill in a real index that does not exceed the diameter
for a target thread engagement, the engagement that drill ACTUALLY produces, the
basic minor diameter, and the surrounding drill sizes with their engagements.
Inputs: thread major diameter, pitch (or threads per inch), target engagement
percentage, unit system, drill index to search.
Key figures: engagement = 100 x (D - d) / (1.299 x P), from the ISO 68-1 basic
profile where H = 0.866025 x P. 100 / 1.299 = 76.98%, which is why the shop rule
"drill = major - pitch" lands just under 77%. Basic minor diameter is
D1 = D - 1.0825 x P and is NOT the tap drill. Standard tap drills do not give a
uniform engagement: M8 on the published 6.8 mm drill gives 73.90%, M12 on 10.2 mm
gives 79.18%, #8-32 on a #29 gives 68.98%.
Jurisdiction: none. ISO metric and Unified inch.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify
